candidates.why_now: #1 real-time Google Trends breakout term today with confirmed news driver; 5+ independent outlets converged in last 24-48h on new Class II classification, a materially new detail beyond original 09-28 dissolution-testing story.
candidates.primary_headline: FDA Says Recalled Blood Pressure Drug Poses 'Class II' Risk — Here's What That Means for Patients
candidates.next_steps: Assign to regulatory/chronic-disease writer; verify FDA.gov recall notice directly before publishing (breaking-recall exception used, confidence capped Medium until confirmed).
integrity_flags: Primary FDA.gov notice not directly retrieved in this run — verify before publication
candidates.trend_score_reason: #1 real-time Google Trends breakout with 5+ secondary outlet convergence in 24-48h on Class II classification detail.
candidates.opportunity_score_reason: High patient-safety relevance and urgency; immediate search interest; strong explainer opportunity (Class II vs. Class I distinction).
candidates.discover_score_reason: Real-time trending term with confirmed news driver and high audience search intent.

candidates.topic: California's new non-UPF food label collides with Stanford Medicine findings that cutting ultra-processed food from school menus is harder than expected
candidates.recommended_angle: Skepticism angle: the policy (non-UPF labeling) just got signed into law days after research shows practical rollout is genuinely difficult — pair the 'why' with the 'how hard.'
candidates.why_now: Two independent tier-1 institutional sources converged same week: Stanford Medicine feasibility study and Governor Newsom's non-UPF labeling law — genuinely new combined story, not previously covered.
candidates.primary_headline: California Just Passed a Law Labeling 'Ultra-Processed' Foods. A New Stanford Study Shows Why Schools Will Struggle to Comply.
candidates.next_steps: Assign to nutrition writer; request RDN quote via Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics on UPF definitional ambiguity.
integrity_flags: Ultra-processed food has no single universally agreed scientific definition — NOVA classification is widely used but contested; flag this ambiguity explicitly
candidates.trend_score_reason: Two tier-1 institutional sources converging same week on same topic (Stanford research + CA policy); moderate trend velocity, strong editorial relevance.
candidates.opportunity_score_reason: High audience value; durable evergreen/Discover potential; clear definitional and practical implementation gap to explore.
candidates.discover_score_reason: Strong evidence-based explainer opportunity with policy + science convergence; high reader engagement potential beyond news cycle.
candidates.notes: Strong evergreen/Discover potential — durable beyond news cycle. Borderline category call passed on audience_relevance and clear evidence angle.

issues: The CA.gov press release describes a broad law creating a 'non-UPF' food label as part of a healthcare strategy package, not a specific mandate requiring schools to remove UPF or comply with a labeling standard — the evidence does not establish that the new law directly obligates school compliance as the headline implies.
The 'collision' framing assumes a direct causal/regulatory link between the Stanford school-food feasibility study and the labeling law that is not substantiated by the two sources cited.
fact_check.checked_against: gov.ca.gov press release on non-UPF label legislation + Stanford Medicine article on ultra-processed school food
